About

Timber has always fascinated me. As a child, I enjoyed watching documentaries about ancient Chinese timber buildings and was amazed by the intelligence behind their structures. As I grew older and learned more about modern engineered wood materials, this curiosity developed into a deeper academic interest.

During my PhD, I explored timber structures through the study of vibration and structural behaviour. I gained experience in hands-on vibration testing, accelerometer data analysis, and numerical verification using MATLAB-based tools. This journey helped me understand that structures are not only about strength and safety, but also about how people experience and interact with them.

I have always been inspired by Nikola Tesla’s words: “If you want to find the secrets of the universe, think in terms of energy, frequency and vibration.” Vibration became the connection between my engineering knowledge and my interest in human experience.

My background in civil engineering taught me to focus on structural elements and connections. However, my PhD gave me a broader perspective—to consider occupant comfort and human perception as equally important as structural performance. This led me to structural serviceability design, especially vibration, where engineering meets human needs.

In the future, I hope to combine traditional materials with modern technologies to create architecture that connects cultural heritage and innovation. Projects such as the Louvre Pyramid show how ancient and modern materials can work together to create meaningful spaces. I believe timber, with its long history and modern potential, can play an important role in this vision.

I am still exploring how to combine thoughtful design with simple, efficient structural solutions—not only to build safe structures, but also to create spaces that connect people, history, and technology.
